title: Communal identity can combine high social trust with partisan alignment and internal educational divides
source_unit: Pew Research Center 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study; U.S. adults with current or former Latter-day Saint identity

denominator.unit: randomly sampled U.S. adults in the Religious Landscape Study; subgroup analyses include 565 current and 316 former Latter-day Saints

communal_engagement.value: membership involves substantial community engagement and Latter-day Saints report strong communal ties

general_social_trust.value: about half say most people can be trusted, placing the group among the more trusting religious groups
general_social_trust.unit: percent of current Latter-day Saint respondents

education_trust_gap.value: six-in-ten with a bachelor's degree versus about four-in-ten without a college diploma say most people can be trusted
education_trust_gap.unit: percent within current Latter-day Saint subgroup

political_identity.value: the group largely identifies as Republican while standing out from partisan peers on selected diversity issues

observations.method: Pew analysis of a large probability-based religious landscape survey with subgroup comparisons of current members, converts, former members, education, trust, communal connection, and political/social attitudes.
observations.uncertainty: The report is descriptive and subgroup margins of error apply. Religious identity, trust, communal ties, and political identity are not a causal chain, and the 2023-24 field period predates the 2026 publication.
observations.subgroup: Current Latter-day Saints, lifelong members, converts, former members, and education groups within the U.S. Religious Landscape Study.
observations.counterinterpretation: High reported trust may reflect selection, social desirability, community structure, or question interpretation; partisan identity does not imply uniform political behavior or agreement on cultural issues.

boundary: This record adds a cultural-identity and trust distribution layer. It does not generalize one religious group to the country, prove that communal ties cause trust or partisan identity, or establish later political action or institutional legitimacy.
